name: Graham Hill
bio: Poet, journalist and playwright; his musical play Havana was a success at the Gaiety in 1908. Five of Wilde's letters to him survive, three of them from 1888, when Hill was about twenty-three and sending Wilde his first book of verse. Wilde read it, criticised one rhyme, praised the touch, teased him about the woman it was dedicated to, and twice asked him to come round. The correspondence resumes in 1891 with the two warmest letters of the five, in which Wilde asks whether he is 'still enamoured of love and poetry' and says he thinks of him often.
bio_note: Added 2026-08-05 under Lovelle's instruction to put friendship on the map as well as romance. NO CONNECTION LINE: what the letters document is an older writer encouraging a younger one. The 2026-08-04 sweep cleared him because its lexicon hit - 'Are you very much in love with M. L.? and does M. L. love you?' - is about a third party, which is right: the editors' note identifies M. L. as Matilda (Minnie) Lloyd, whom Hill later married. But the letters around that line are warm and are recorded here. ALL FIVE LETTERS have been read at the page: three at printed 380 (repo PDF 402), then printed 480 (PDF 500) and printed 483 (PDF 503), every folio confirmed on its own page image. The last two are from 1891, three years after the first three, and are the warmest — 'I wish I saw you oftener' and 'I often think of you, and am sorry we meet so rarely'. Dates 1865-1933 from the editors' note at printed 380.

context_engagements.note: Mentorship and friendship. All three 1888 letters are quoted entire - none contains anything that does not bear on the two of them, so nothing is elided.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Hill, Come and have tea on Friday at 5 o'clock if you have nothing to do. So you are a rhymer! We all are when we are young. Believe me truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to Graham Hill, [? 1888], 16 Tite Street (MS Mason) - the first of the three letters printed together on this page.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The invitation, and the terms of the friendship: an established writer amused by a young one.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 402; printed folio 380 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05. Quoted whole.

sources.quote: My dear Graham Hill, I am charmed with your little volume; the triolets, ballades, and rondeaus are very graceful and dainty. I am sorry you have rhymed 'tears' to 'ideas' in your envoy; rhymes of this kind are very wicked, but you certainly have a light touch and a pleasant fancy. The book is very prettily got up, and 'M. L.', whoever she is, should feel quite proud at such an artistic offering. Are you very much in love with M. L.? and does M. L. love you? Come and see me some day. Wednesday afternoon usually finds me in. Truly yours
sources.context: The second letter on the same page, on Hill's Under Her Window (1888). The editors' note 3 identifies 'M. L.' as Matilda (Minnie) Lloyd, whom Hill later married - the line the 2026-08-04 sweep correctly read as being about a third party. It is quoted here in its place in the letter rather than on its own, because on its own it is the only thing anyone has noticed about this correspondence.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde reading a young poet's book closely, praising and correcting it, teasing him about his sweetheart, and asking him to call.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 402; printed folio 380 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05. Quoted whole.

sources.quote: Dear Graham Hill, I don't think that poems are ever really helped by the publication of letters from private friends. An anonymous criticism is always something, or supposed to be something, but personal letters are different. However you are quite at liberty to do as you think best. I hope you will be successful in whatever branch of literature you take up, and am very glad you are turning your attention to prose. Good prose is what we want. How is your journalism progressing? Truly yours
sources.context: The third letter on the same page. Hill had evidently asked to print Wilde's praise; Wilde declines the use and encourages the career in the same breath.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The shape of the friendship - Wilde withholding his name from Hill's publicity while backing his work.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 402; printed folio 380 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05. Quoted whole.

sources.quote: Your paper is charming – it was kind of you to send it to me. I never write for newspapers now, but if I have at any future time something suitable you shall have it. I wish I saw you oftener. Sincerely yours … Write yourself a review of Dorian Gray.
sources.context: Wilde to Graham Hill, [? May 1891], 16 Tite Street (MS Mason) — quoted whole, postscript included. The editors could not identify the paper Hill was writing for, and record that no review of Dorian Gray by him has ever been traced.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Three years on from the first letters, the friendship still running — and Wilde saying plainly that he would like to see more of him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 500; printed folio 480 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.

sources.quote: Thank you so much for the cutting which amused me very much. How are you getting on? Are you still enamoured of love and poetry? I hope so. They are the only two things in the world that remain. I often think of you, and am sorry we meet so rarely. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to Graham Hill, [? Summer 1891], Lyric Club, Piccadilly East (MS Mason) — the last of the five, quoted whole, and the warmest.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The closest thing to a declaration in this correspondence: 'I often think of you, and am sorry we meet so rarely.'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 503; printed folio 483 confirmed on the rendered page image, read 2026-08-05.
